summary: A 1971 note by R. M. Metcalfe with some historic moments in networking.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 89 describes early experiments that connected an MIT terminal to Multics and Harvard, then used the network to run a graphics program at MITDG. The report also records difficulties with terminal characters, input handling and response time.

questions: how did early networks handle remote terminals
what were the first network experiments
how did the arpanet support graphics
what is an ncp network control program
subtitle: Reports of remote terminal and graphics experiments between MIT, Multics and Harvard.

tldr.problem: The MITDG group wanted to demonstrate remote terminal access and exchange of programs and data while its interim network control program was being completed.
tldr.mechanism: The experiments used an interim interim NCP to connect terminals to Multics and Harvard, and to send a graphics program and data between Harvard and MITDG.
tldr.outcome: The report describes successful experiments along with character, buffering and response-time problems that remained.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 89 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text documents experiments and the technical issues observed while they were performed.

sections.title: Experiments with the Interim NCP
sections.content:
While waiting for an interim network control program (INCP), the MITDG PDP-6/10 group used an interim interim NCP (IINCP). The IINCP treated the IMP interface as a single-user input/output device for raw network messages, with basic interrupt handling and buffering.

The report says programs were written close to the hardware and had to account for the IMP-Host protocol, including RFNMs and startup NOPs.
sections.plainLanguage: MITDG used a small interim program to exchange raw network messages before the planned control program was ready. That meant the experiment's programs had to handle details normally intended for the network software.

sections.title: Connecting to Multics and Harvard
sections.content:
The first experiment connected an MITDG terminal to a Multics process. The systems differed in their terminal behavior: Multics expected line-oriented, half-duplex input, while MITDG was character-oriented. The report describes handling line endings and local RUBOUT editing, and notes that a remote QUIT function was missing.

The Harvard connection exposed different meanings for control-C and control-Z on the Harvard DEC system and MIT's ITS. The report also describes the Harvard pseudo-teletype's half-duplex behavior and says the response seemed as fast as expected despite several systems and IMPs in the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote terminals worked, but each system handled typing and control characters differently. The experiments had to account for those differences to make a user session work.

sections.title: A Harvard-MIT Graphics Experiment
sections.content:
Harvard sent a PDP-10 core image containing a program to MITDG. MITDG placed the image in memory, ran its graphics program on the Evans & Sutherland line-drawing system and sent the result to Harvard's PDP-1 for display.

The report says the display changed on the order of twice each second, perhaps less often, and was limited by transmission. It also records garbled IMP-teletype messages and an intermittent connection failure during bidirectional transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Harvard sent a program to MITDG, where it ran on a graphics system. MITDG sent the resulting display data back to Harvard, though the report notes limited speed and intermittent problems.

sections.title: Issues the Experiments Exposed
sections.content:
The report discusses message marking and padding, differing terminal conventions and the limits of response time for dynamic graphics. It notes that more bandwidth, faster host response or message priorities might be needed to improve real-time graphics.

Metcalfe presents the work as experiments and invites participation in further experiments; the report does not describe a final general-purpose protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The experiments showed that remote programs and graphics could work, but also exposed limits in speed and compatibility. The author invites further experiments rather than claiming all problems are solved.
